messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos is a 40-year-old vascular surgeon, a man whose hands had held the delicate threads of human life for over a decade. The trauma, however, had not occurred in an operating room. It had happened in his own home, during a wildfire that swept through his suburban neighborhood two years ago. He had been off-duty, asleep, when the smoke alarm screamed him into a world of orange light and suffocating heat. He remembered the roar, the way the smoke had felt like a physical weight pressing him into the floorboards as he crawled to his wife’s room. He had gotten them out, but the memory that haunted him most was not the fire itself—it was the moment in the driveway, looking back at the house, when he realized he could not remember if he had checked the guest room where his elderly mother had been staying. She had been at a neighbor’s, safe, but the *not knowing* in that single, frozen second had carved a fault line into his mind. That incomplete picture—the gap where a life-or-death decision should have been—was the crack through which everything else now leaked.

Now, something as simple as the burnt toast his wife made on Sunday mornings could undo him. The smell would hit his nostrils, and without any warning, he would be back in that hallway, the roar in his ears, his heart slamming against his ribs. The auditory trigger was just as potent; a car backfiring in the hospital parking lot could make him flinch so violently that a scrub nurse once asked if he was okay. These triggers did not just bring the memory back; they *were* the memory, a full sensory assault. And the more the memory intruded, the more sensitive he became to its cues. He had started to notice the smell of smoke everywhere—in the dry-cleaning return, in the exhaust of a bus—and each time, the loop tightened. He would be standing at the scrub sink, and the faintest hint of a burnt smell from the cautery in the OR would flood his senses, and he would feel a wave of grief so profound it left him breathless, a sorrow for the house, for the life before, for the terrifying blank spot in his own recollection.

To manage this, Carlos had developed a set of private strategies. In the evenings, after a long case, he would pour himself a glass of whiskey, then another, telling himself it was to steady his hands for the next day. The alcohol helped, briefly, by blurring the edges of the intrusive images. He also found that losing himself in a complex video game or a surgical journal was a reliable form of distraction; if he kept his mind fully occupied, the gaps in his memory felt less threatening. More privately, and with a deep sense of shame, he had begun to use sexual fantasies as a way to discharge the coiled tension in his body, a quick, solitary pressure release before sleep. These strategies worked in the moment, but they carried a hidden cost. The alcohol, in particular, seemed to make his sleep more fragmented, and on those restless nights, the incomplete memory of the fire would surface again, more fragmented and more terrifying than before. The distraction and the drinking were not truly containing the memory; they were, in a way, feeding it, ensuring that when it did break through, it did so with the force of something long held back.

The most significant consequence, however, was in his marriage. He had become distant, irritable. After a day of being hyper-vigilant for any burnt smell in the hospital—a smell that could instantly trigger a cascade of memory and grief—he would come home exhausted, pour his drink, and retreat into his phone or a film. His wife, who had survived the fire with him, wanted to talk, to process, but Carlos was certain that if he opened that door, the grief would drown him. He had come to believe that his mind was broken, that the missing piece of that memory meant he was fundamentally unreliable. He avoided the topic of the fire entirely, and his wife had begun to sleep in the guest room, interpreting his withdrawal as a rejection. It was only when a young intern mentioned, offhand, that she had nightmares about a code she’d lost, that Carlos realized he had not spoken a single word about the fire in over a year. He is seeking help now not because he wants to relive the event, but because he is terrified that the strategies he has built to survive it are slowly dismantling the only life he has left. He hopes, above all, to find a way to remember the fire without being consumed by it, and to stop the grief from being the only thing he feels when he looks at his wife.
